name: Napping / NSDR / yoga nidra
lead: Napping, non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) and yoga nidra are short rest practices used to recover energy, reduce stress and make up for lost sleep. A nap is a short daytime sleep; yoga nidra is a guided, lying-down meditation often described as a state between waking and sleeping; NSDR is a newer label for similar guided-rest protocols.[1][2] In looksmaxxing communities they are used as part of a recovery routine meant to support how a person looks: more rested eyes and skin, better training recovery and more alertness and energy.[7][13]

Forum authors describe naps as an overlooked recovery tool, arguing that short midday sleep supports alertness, memory and training recovery, and some tie rest to aesthetics through a fresher, less tired appearance.[7] Athletic-performance research gives a related picture: a 2021 narrative review examined how daytime napping affects athletic performance.[8]
Research on naps reports benefits for alertness and memory, and early trials of yoga nidra report effects on sleep, stress and mood in small groups.[1][2][9][10]

chain: Short nap or guided rest between waking hours
Less sleep debt and lower stress
More energy and training recovery, fresher-looking face
angle.text: People use naps and guided rest to offset short nights and support training and daily energy. Practitioners link better-rested days with a fresher look and better workout recovery.

infobox: Micro 2-5 min, power 10-30 min, full cycle about 90 min[1]

paras: Naps are categorised by duration, such as micro naps of a few minutes, power naps of 10-30 minutes and full-cycle naps of about 90 minutes.[1] Wikipedia reports that early afternoon is when sleepiness typically peaks and describes 20-30 minutes as a common recommendation for adults.[1] A NASA study is reported to show a 26-minute nap improved alertness by 54% and performance by 34% in pilots.[1]

Sleep inertia, the grogginess after waking, is more likely after longer naps that reach slow-wave sleep and rarely lasts beyond 30 minutes in people who are not sleep-deprived.[1] A 2016 meta-analysis linked habitual naps over an hour with higher cardiovascular and metabolic risk, with no causal link established, while naps up to 40 minutes showed no such association.[1] Sleep in general aids memory consolidation.[3]

Yoga nidra's modern form draws on Western relaxation methods; Satyananda Saraswati popularised a structured method in 1976, and Richard Miller developed iRest for soldiers with PTSD.[2] Claimed benefits include reduced anxiety and better sleep; a small trial of 45 male athletes found improved sleep latency and efficiency versus progressive muscle relaxation.[2]
NSDR is a newer name for similar guided-rest protocols and is not covered in Wikipedia's yoga nidra article.[2]

One looksmax.org thread presents the power nap as a forgotten part of recovery, describing short naps as improving reaction time, attention and memory consolidation, and warning that long naps can leave users groggy.[7] Replies in the thread mention sleeping for hours when attempting a nap and using phone alarms to limit it.[7] A separate thread discusses social perceptions of men napping.[12]

Nap research includes the NASA pilot study and the 2016 meta-analysis.[1] A 2021 narrative review examined daytime napping and athletic performance.[8] A Zurich crossover study in 70 healthy women found that a hypnotic suggestion to sleep deeper, played before a 90-minute nap, increased slow-wave sleep by 81 percent.[4]

Yoga nidra trials include a randomized sleep-lab feasibility study in 22 adults with self-reported insomnia,[5] a randomized trial in chronic insomnia,[6] and trials on stress and self-esteem in university students[9] and on anxiety and insomnia in COVID-19 frontline health workers.[10] No studies were found on NSDR as a named protocol.

timeline.event: Dennis Boyes uses 'yoga nidra' in a French book.[2]
US Army Surgeon General endorses yoga nidra for chronic pain as complementary medicine.[2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org naps and rest appear within sleep-and-recovery discussions as a way to support performance and appearance.[7]

claims.claim: Power naps improve recovery, performance and aesthetics
claims.believers: A looksmax.org author says mid-day naps improve reaction time, attention, decision-making and memory and describes recovery and aesthetic benefits.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports benefits for alertness and memory from naps, and a narrative review examined naps and athletic performance; no studies were found on naps and facial appearance.[1][8]

claims.believers: The same author reports napping for too long left him feeling worse.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes sleep inertia as more likely after longer naps and reports a 2016 meta-analysis associating habitual naps over an hour with higher risk markers, without establishing causation.[1]

claims.claim: Guided rest such as yoga nidra improves sleep and lowers stress
claims.believers: Practitioners describe yoga nidra as deeply relaxing and sleep-supporting.[2]
claims.experts: Small randomized trials report effects on insomnia and stress outcomes.[5][6][9]

card.summary: Short naps and guided deep-rest sessions for recovery; naps have decent evidence, yoga nidra is promising but small.
card.note: Long habitual naps associated with health risks in observational data.

quick.overview:
These are brief rest practices: daytime naps, and guided relaxation known as yoga nidra or NSDR.

Naps show benefits for alertness and learning, while yoga nidra research is small.
quick.mechanism: Naps restore alertness through short sleep; yoga nidra uses guided body awareness to produce deep relaxation.
quick.risks: Long naps can cause grogginess, and habitual long napping is linked observationally with health risks.
